## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{100}{0}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can training on a useful recovery record teach the model to repeat the mistake instead of the correction?_

Fine-tuning changes the model itself, and its effects persist in every call the policy makes afterward. A clearer context, a corrected tool schema, or a stricter runtime check can each be tested against the failing cases and withdrawn in a single release. A weight change needs a corpus, a training run, and a fresh evaluation, and it is undone only by another release. The records that feed it also differ from the text a language model first learned from. An agent trajectory has two authors. The model proposes calls and reports, and the environment answers with results, errors, and refusals. A recovery record interleaves a mistake, the evidence that exposed it, and the correction, and only part of that record is behavior the policy should learn to produce. A pipeline that blurs these roles can lower its training loss while teaching the policy to repeat the mistake or to invent the tool output it should have waited for, and the loss curve never shows the difference. Taking the distinction seriously turns fine-tuning from a routine training job into a discipline of choosing targets, preserving what each response was conditioned on, and demanding closed-loop evidence before release. It also fixes where learning sits in the agent. Training moves none of the H·S·A exposures; it changes the policy that proposes actions, while the horizon, state, and authority bounds enforced by the runtime hold whatever the new weights propose.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Assign agent behavior to weights, context, or runtime, and decide when a failure warrants a weight change
- Construct model inputs that preserve intended conditioning and price per-invocation serialization in training tokens
- Map admitted response spans to causal token targets, observation masks, and termination policy
- Compare loss weighting and construct batches without unintended cross-example dependencies
- Calculate imitation regret bounds on reference and learner states to decide when on-policy labeling pays
- Calculate preference margins and gradient weights, and distinguish what a comparison measures from task acceptance
- Select behavior sources and parameter artifacts using explicit resource and version accounting
- Evaluate a versioned policy for release while preserving runtime enforcement and scoped acceptance criteria

:::

## Recovery Records as Training Data {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-introduction}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with no axis highlighted and the origin dot highlighted in purple."}

*Fine-tuning reshapes each model call but leaves every exposure to the runtime.*
:::

The curation pipeline has admitted a recovery demonstration from the repair agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) to `repair_demonstrations_v1`. In that hypothetical record, a malformed edit proposal was refused before dispatch, the model inspected the schema, and a corrected edit produced candidate `ws_r20`. The selected policy responses are the schema inspection request, the corrected edit, and the scoped final report. The malformed proposal and the delivered check result remain context. Curation has justified those selections and recorded them as a target policy, `recovery_targets_v1`.

An admitted record is not yet something a training job can consume. The event log holds what the runtime retained, in the order it happened, with the model's messages and the environment's replies side by side. A loader that treats every model message as a target trains the malformed proposal along with its correction. One that trains every token asks the model to predict test output it will never have to write. One that mixes this record with unrelated examples in a shared buffer can let those examples read the repair's file contents. Each of these mistakes lowers a training loss, and none of them shows up in it. The evaluation contract built so far measures a running agent, and the curation contract decides which responses are worth learning; neither says how a selected response becomes a gradient.

This chapter builds that path, from an admitted record to an identified, evaluated policy update. It starts by fixing what a weight change can and cannot alter, which bounds everything that follows. It then turns the record into model inputs that reproduce what each selected response was conditioned on, a loss mask that trains those responses and nothing else, and batches whose weighting and boundaries leave the learning problem unchanged. A faithful update still meets states and interfaces its corpus never showed, so the chapter next measures that coverage gap and the data that closes it. Three further choices, the objective, the source of the behavior, and the parameter artifact that is trained and shipped, can each change independently. The chapter ends with the evidence a candidate needs before it replaces the policy in service.

@Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-scope sorts agent behavior among weights, context, and runtime. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking, and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching build the training example, its targets, and its batches. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-exposure-bias and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-schemas address the states and schemas the trained policy meets on its own. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dpo, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation, and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-peft take the objective, the behavior source, and the parameter artifact in turn. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-benchmarking evaluates the candidate, and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-synthesis assembles the whole path into a training manifest for the repair policy.

## Scope of Supervised Fine-Tuning {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-scope}

Changing weights is the right intervention only for a particular kind of failure. The intervention ordering of @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order tries cheap, reversible fixes first: the context the model receives, then the tool schemas it calls against, then the runtime checks around it. Each of those can be tested against the failing cases and reverted in one release. A weight change needs a corpus, a training run, and a fresh evaluation before it can be trusted, and it is undone only by another release. Fine-tuning is therefore the intervention for the residual failure that survives those fixes, a recurring behavior pattern that evidence attributes to the policy rather than to missing information or a missing check. Verified trajectory post-training (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training})\index{Principle!verified trajectory post-training} makes that comparison part of admitting a record for learning. The ordering is a default justified by cost and reversibility; @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation treats the case where training is cheaper than carrying the same guidance in every prompt.

**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**\index{Supervised fine-tuning!definition} adjusts trainable model parameters to increase the likelihood of selected target tokens under their supplied prefixes. For the admitted derived record `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, that means implementing `recovery_targets_v1` without turning every recorded model message into a target. The model must receive the information that makes each selected response appropriate, but not later evidence that would reveal the answer prematurely. Training therefore inherits both a target-selection contract and a conditioning contract.

This distinction gives a concrete meaning to better behavior. The intended lesson is to inspect the current schema after the represented refusal, issue a supported correction, and report what the available check establishes. Memorizing this fixture's paths or predicting its test output would fit the record without learning that lesson, and whether the learned policy applies the lesson on other tasks is what @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-benchmarking measures.

### Procedure, contracts, and enforcement {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-behavior-homes}

Every response the model produces is a function of two inputs, the weights and the context assembled for that call. Fine-tuning changes only the first. That fact sorts what an agent needs into three homes, summarized in @tbl-vol3-fine-tuning-scope. *Procedure* is behavior that holds across tasks and changes slowly, such as inspecting diagnostic evidence before editing and checking what remains unresolved before reporting completion. Procedure is what the weights can learn. *Contracts* are the facts that vary across deployments and calls, such as tool definitions, task requirements, and granted scope. They stay in context, because a model that memorized last month's schema emits last month's arguments. *Enforcement* is whatever must hold when the model is wrong, such as validation, authorization, and containment. It stays in the runtime under the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

| Home    | Intended responsibility                                                                    | Consequence for fine-tuning                                                                                                      |
|:--------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Weights | Learned procedures and response tendencies, including tool selection and recovery behavior | Update the proposal distribution, then measure whether the changed behavior helps under the declared task conditions             |
| Context | Current task facts, tool schemas, observations, and represented scope                      | Supply the information the policy needs now; do not rely on memorized versions as the authority for current facts or permissions |
| Runtime | Validation, authorization, containment, resource controls, and evidence collection         | Preserve enforcement independently of the learned policy; a model's predicted result is not an observed external effect          |

: **Responsibilities of Weights, Context, and Runtime**: Weights hold procedure, context holds the current contract, and the runtime enforces that contract whatever the model proposes. {#tbl-vol3-fine-tuning-scope}

A memorized schema is a stale contract. A changed interface may require a new argument, and a revoked permission stays revoked however often training demonstrated the old action, so what training can usefully teach is the habit of consulting the supplied contract.

The sorting rules out a tempting description of fine-tuning as moving the whole prompt into the weights. Only the procedural part of a prompt, such as a debugging checklist or few-shot recovery examples, can move into the weights, saving those tokens on every turn (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation). The contractual part must stay, because removing it leaves the model guessing at the facts of the current task, and the check that enforces a permission moves into neither prompt nor weights.

Fine-tuning does change which tools the model requests, how long it investigates, and which environment states it reaches, and those changes can improve or worsen task outcomes and resource use. All of them play out inside the horizon, state, and authority bounds the runtime sets. We call this the *proposal boundary*. Training changes what the policy proposes, and it never changes what the runtime permits. Every later section relies on it, including the release decision at the chapter's end.

### Objective, behavior source, and artifact {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-adaptation-choices}

The remaining design choices answer different questions. The objective specifies the training signal. Imitation rewards selected responses, while preference learning compares alternatives under a justified preference. The behavior source specifies where examples and their conditioning come from, such as reviewed collection runs or a teacher configuration. The parameter artifact specifies what is trained and released, such as full weights or an adapter associated with a base model. The three choices combine freely, so a single adapter can carry a preference objective trained on teacher-generated examples. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dpo, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation, and @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-peft take them in turn.

None of these choices matters until the admitted record becomes a model input. Serialization fixes the tokens and visible context, masking selects the predictions to train, and batching sets their weighting and dependencies. The trained policy then meets states and schemas the record never showed, and an identified artifact must pass evaluation before release. The first step is constructing the input each selected response is conditioned on.

## Serializing Trajectories {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization}

The admitted repair demonstration contains a malformed edit proposal, its refusal, a schema inspection, and a corrected edit. A training loader that deletes the refusal changes the problem the correction answers. A loader that places the later passing check before the edit gives the model evidence that was unavailable when it chose the edit. Curation selected the responses; serialization must reconstruct the inputs they answered, including the record's redaction (a substituted path that was never executed), whose status the training example carries forward.

### Reconstructing each model input {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-input-reconstruction}

An event log records what the runtime retained, which can be less than the complete input of a model call. The delivered-input manifests from @sec-vol3-persistence-replay identify which messages, tool definitions, summaries, and bounded observations the model received, with their contents and versions. The manifest, rather than an event timestamp, is the evidence that a payload entered a particular invocation.

For a historical-fidelity example, reconstruct the selected invocation from its available input record. Preserve the actual visible observation, including its partial-result status, rather than replacing it with a fuller result obtained later. For an intentionally transformed example, apply the reviewed transformation to that input and its associated response, preserve the parent references, and recheck their compatibility. A shortened prompt for context distillation is such a transformation, developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation.

@Tbl-vol3-serialization-repair-spans follows the response selection already admitted for the repair. The entries describe content relationships; the rendered example supplies the full retained context of each selected invocation, including task instructions and current tool definitions.

| Selected response | Relevant conditioning evidence                                                                      | Response content selected by curation                |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `e3`              | Earlier delivered task context and the malformed `e2` proposal with its pre-dispatch refusal        | Request to inspect the available schema              |
| `e4`              | The corresponding returned schema and the retained context supporting the edit                      | Corrected edit with its version condition            |
| `e6`              | The candidate-specific check summary delivered at `e5` and retained evidence for the report's scope | Final report of the supported result and limitations |

: **Inputs and Selected Responses in the Repair Demonstration**: Each row pairs a reviewed response with evidence available to condition it. {#tbl-vol3-serialization-repair-spans}

The refusal at `e2` is runtime evidence that dispatch never happened, rather than the output of an executed edit. The check summary at `e5` arrived after the edit, so it conditions the report at `e6` and only that report. Selecting the schema request at `e3` selects the request alone; the schema its tool returned stays observation. Keeping those associations explicit lets the next section construct a mask over the intended responses rather than over entire exchanges.

### Rendering with versioned templates {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-template-rendering}

Structured messages must become the token sequence expected by the chosen model. Templates differ in how they represent roles, tool calls, and message endings, even between models derived from the same base. Record the tokenizer and template versions, tool-definition formatting, and response-boundary policy with the serialized artifact. The model input is the message list together with that configuration.

In schematic form, one multi-turn tool-calling example has the following shape. The delimiter spellings are placeholders, since each template spells them differently. The system segment carries the task contract and tool schemas, the assistant segment carries an optional rationale and two parallel calls with identifiers, and each tool segment carries one result keyed to the call it answers.

```text
<|system|> task contract; schemas for read_file(target_uri), run_tests(target) <|end|>
<|user|> Fix the connection-pool leak in src/pool.py <|end|>
<|assistant|> <|reasoning|> Reproduce the failure, then read the module. <|end_reasoning|>
  <|call id=c1|> {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"target_uri": "src/pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
  <|call id=c2|> {"name": "run_tests", "arguments": {"target": "tests/test_pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
<|end_turn|>
<|tool id=c2|> FAILED test_release: pool exhausted <|end|>
<|tool id=c1|> ...file contents... <|end|>
<|assistant|> ...
```

Here `c2` returns before `c1`, and the identifiers keep each result bound to its request. Presentation order follows the input assembly rather than completion order, and reordering calls whose arguments or observations depend on one another changes the problem, so any reordering is a declared data transformation with its own justification. The `<|end_turn|>` marker is the policy's own act of yielding control to the runtime; everything between `<|tool|>` and `<|end|>` is observation.

Call the illustrative artifact `serialization_v1`. Its manifest binds the admitted record and target-selection version to the chosen rendering configuration and maps each selected response span into the resulting tokens. Rendering or redaction can move token boundaries, so every offset is rechecked against the final rendering. Decode or inspect the completed examples to verify the task context, call/result associations, selected response boundaries, and real termination markers. An example with missing content or a failed alignment check is dropped from this use rather than patched with invented content.

Role markers describe the input protocol and confer no authority. Generated text that resembles a tool message remains model output under any delimiter scheme, and serialization never promotes it into an observation (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-role).

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-per-turn-expansion
#| echo: false
# PER-TURN EXAMPLE EXPANSION (LEGO)
# Goal: Price one-example-per-invocation serialization against one transcript.
# Scope: Stipulated horizon; each turn adds a similar number of tokens.
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class PerTurnExpansion:
    # 1. LOAD: stipulated horizon in turns.
    horizon = 30

    # 2. EXECUTE: prefixes of 1..H turns versus one H-turn transcript.
    per_turn_units = horizon * (horizon + 1) / 2
    transcript_units = horizon
    expansion = per_turn_units / transcript_units

    # 3. GUARD: closed form (H+1)/2.
    check(abs(expansion - (horizon + 1) / 2) < 1e-12, "Expansion is (H+1)/2")
    check(expansion > 1, "Separate examples repeat context")

    # 4. OUTPUT: consumed in the serialization prose.
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    expansion_mult_str = fmt_multiple(expansion, precision=1)
```

Some serving policies retain earlier generated text; others omit or summarize it before later invocations. A single concatenated transcript is a faithful example only when its attention-visible prefixes match what serving delivered. Otherwise each invocation becomes its own example with its own prefix, and the repeated context has a price. If each of $H$ turns adds about $L$ tokens, the example for turn $k$ carries about $kL$, so the $H$ examples hold about $L\,H(H+1)/2$ tokens against $LH$ for one transcript, an expansion of $(H+1)/2$. At a stipulated horizon of `{python} PerTurnExpansion.horizon_str` turns, the same trajectory costs `{python} PerTurnExpansion.expansion_mult_str` the training tokens, which makes serving's reasoning-retention policy a first-order input to sizing the run. Reconstruction includes only rationale that serving actually delivered, under the declared input and target policy.

`serialization_v1` now identifies the tokenized examples, their conditioning evidence, and the spans eligible under curation's selection. The next decision is which token predictions contribute to the objective. Observation loss masking converts that span selection into aligned prediction targets while leaving necessary observations available as context.

## Observation Loss Masking {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking}

A loader that selects every assistant token would train the malformed proposal along with its correction, undoing the curation decision. A loader that selects every token would also ask the policy to predict the environment's responses. Serialization defines the input; the loss mask must implement the intended target selection on that input.

### The masked objective {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-masked-objective}

Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$ be one serialized example, with an initial context or boundary token at $x_1$. Let $\mathcal{P}_{\text{elig}}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,T\}$ contain the eligible policy-token positions selected for imitation. Eligibility depends on the admitted response spans and the training objective, not authorship alone. The mask is $m_t=\mathbf{1}\{t\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{elig}}\}$, with $m_1=0$. For an example with at least one selected target, the mean masked cross-entropy is

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{active}}}\sum_{t=2}^{T}m_t\log P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}),\qquad N_{\mathrm{active}}=\sum_{t=2}^{T}m_t>0.$$ {#eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective}

Each selected token is predicted from the preceding prefix. The training computation uses the recorded preceding tokens, including earlier selected responses, rather than sampling a fresh continuation at every position. This is **teacher forcing**\index{Teacher forcing!definition}[^fn-teacher-forcing-origin] [@williams1989learning]. It can include recovery prefixes containing mistakes, provided those inputs and targets passed the curation contract.

[^fn-teacher-forcing-origin]: **Teacher Forcing**: Williams and Zipser named the technique in 1989 for recurrent networks, feeding the recorded target back as the next input instead of the network's own output. Because every prefix is recorded rather than generated, a causal model computes all of an example's next-token predictions in one parallel forward pass, which is why imitating a trajectory costs one pass per example rather than one sampled rollout per decision.

In the repair example, `target_mask_v1` maps the reviewed response spans onto the tokens produced by `serialization_v1`, distinguishing selected targets from conditioning input as in @tbl-vol3-loss-masking-strata. A changed tokenizer, template, or transformed input can change those positions, so the mask must be regenerated and checked against the corresponding serialization rather than copied by stale offsets.

| Token segment                                              | Target policy for this imitation objective                                                 | What remains as conditioning input                                                   |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Prompt and supplied tool contracts                         | $m_t=0$                                                                                    | The actual task, current interfaces, and supplied constraints                        |
| Selected policy response                                   | $m_t=1$ on its admitted target positions                                                   | Earlier tokens of the response and its available prefix                              |
| Unselected policy response, including the refused proposal | $m_t=0$                                                                                    | History needed to interpret a selected correction                                    |
| Tool or environment observation                            | $m_t=0$                                                                                    | Delivered results, errors, and evidence available before the next response           |
| Optional authorized rationale                              | Chosen by the declared target policy                                                       | Retained rationale remains visible whether or not it is selected                     |
| Termination boundary                                       | Select an authentic policy-generated terminator when teaching the selected response to end | Do not substitute a tool-role boundary or invent a terminator for a cut-off response |

: **Loss Masking by Token Segment**: The mask implements a learning-use decision on the serialized input. It is neither an authority check nor an attention mask. {#tbl-vol3-loss-masking-strata}

An example with no selected targets has no defined mean in @eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective. The pipeline excludes it from this objective, or handles it under an explicitly defined aggregation policy, and never counts it as a trained demonstration. Batch-level weighting is a separate choice developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching.

::: {#dfn-action-loss-masking .callout-definition title="Observation loss masking"}

***Observation loss masking***\index{Observation loss masking!definition}\index{Supervised fine-tuning!loss masking} excludes supplied observations from the direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted observation context needed to train selected policy responses.

1. **Significance**: It keeps the whole objective on the policy's conditional distribution $P(a_t\mid s_t)$, so observation text, however much of a trajectory it fills, cannot dilute the weight on the responses the policy must learn (notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} prices the dilution).
2. **Distinction**: A masked token stays in the input and is read through attention; only its direct prediction loss is removed. Policy authorship alone does not make a token a desired target.
3. **Common pitfall**: Selecting an entire tool exchange because its request was admitted, thereby selecting the environment's reply as well.

:::

### Causal label alignment {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-label-alignment}

In a causal language model,[^fn-causal-mask-shift] logits produced after input position $t-1$ predict token $x_t$. A loader must therefore align those logits with label $x_t$ and mask $m_t$, not with the mask of the input token at $t-1$. @Tbl-vol3-mask-causal-shift makes the boundary cases explicit. Some training interfaces perform this shift internally; applying it again in the loader misaligns the targets. Inspect the actual labels and predictions on a short example before training a corpus.

[^fn-causal-mask-shift]: **Causal Self-Attention**: The Transformer decoder masks each position's attention to later positions so that training on a whole sequence cannot read the tokens it is asked to predict [@vaswani2017]. The mask is what lets one forward pass produce every next-token prediction at once, and it is also why labels must be shifted by one position: the hidden state at $t-1$ is the only place the prediction of $x_t$ exists.

| Logits computed from a prefix ending at…          | Next-token label                          | Target mask |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------|
| The final supplied prompt token                   | First token of a selected policy response | $1$         |
| The final content token of that selected response | Its authentic policy-generated end token  | $1$         |
| The end token before a delivered tool observation | First token of that observation           | $0$         |

: **The Causal Label Shift at a Tool Boundary**: Selection belongs to the predicted token, not the token whose hidden state produces the prediction. Actual boundary spellings follow the versioned template. {#tbl-vol3-mask-causal-shift}

Let $o_{t-1,v}$ denote the logit for vocabulary token $v$ produced from $x_{<t}$, using an ordinary softmax and no label smoothing. Differentiating @eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective gives

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}{\partial o_{t-1,v}}=\frac{m_t}{N_{\mathrm{active}}}\left(P_\theta(v\mid x_{<t})-\mathbf{1}\{v=x_t\}\right).$$

When $m_t=0$, that next-token prediction supplies no direct loss derivative. The token still shapes later selected predictions through attention, and gradients from those later losses update the parameters that encode it. A masked observation is read and learned from, but never imitated. That is how verified trajectory post-training (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}) reaches the level of individual tokens.

The mask exists because a trajectory has two authors. Unmasked training asks one set of weights to fit two conditional distributions. One is the policy, $P(a_t\mid s_t)$, which maps what the agent has seen to its next response. The other is an environment model, $P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$, which predicts what a shell, compiler, or service will return. In an agent with real tools the second is redundant, because the tool is present at every turn and returns its own output.

Fitting the environment model anyway has two costs. The first is **loss dilution**\index{Loss dilution!definition}. Under token averaging, unmasking raises the denominator from $N_{\mathrm{active}}$ to nearly $T$, so each selected target's coefficient falls by the selected share of the input, which notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} computes for one example. The remaining weight goes to observation text such as paths, identifiers, and log lines, much of which no policy could predict. The second is **role confusion**\index{Role confusion!definition}. A model trained to predict the text that follows a call learns that tool-like output follows a call. At deployment it can then continue past its own call with an invented result instead of emitting the terminator that yields the turn. The runtime rejects such a turn, because generated text is model output rather than an observation (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization), and each rejection spends a turn of the budget. @Fig-vol3-loss-masking lays the mask over the repair example's segments and separates the two paths by which a token reaches the parameters.

::: {#fig-vol3-loss-masking fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Observation Loss Masking**: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). Of the segments shown, only the corrected tool call and the final response carry $m_t=1$ and receive a direct loss term. The prompt, task, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry $m_t=0$, yet every one of them is still read through attention, so gradients from later selected targets update the parameters that encode it. Selecting only policy responses fits the policy's conditional distribution; unmasking the observations would also ask the same weights to fit the environment's." fig-alt="Seven serialized segments in a row: prompt and tool contracts, task statement, refused proposal, rejection message, corrected tool call, tool result, and final response with end token. Below each is its loss mask, zero for all except the corrected tool call and the final response, which are one. A direct loss row marks only those two as imitated. A context row spans all segments, stating they are read through attention and updated by gradients of later selected targets. At the bottom, one box pairs selected targets with the policy P of a t given s t, and a dashed box pairs unmasked observations with the environment P of s t plus 1 given s t and a t."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-loss-masking.svg)
:::

The mask removes both mechanisms. How often a given unmasked model fabricates results is a closed-loop measurement that the loss curve cannot reveal. Environment-text prediction is a legitimate objective for a different purpose, such as training a simulator of the tools, and a separate one from the policy imitation this chapter builds.

### Selected targets and compute {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-selected-targets}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_sft_margin_targets.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal stacked bar. A long green segment labeled observations 77.1% fills most of it, a gray segment labeled ctx follows, and a thin dark segment at the right end is labeled targets 4.9%."}

*Observations fill 77.1 percent of the input; the loss sits on 4.9 percent.*
:::

The number of selected positions sets the denominator of this loss and therefore the coefficient each selected token receives. Long observations can fill most of an input while serving as context for a short corrective response, so the selected share of stored tokens measures how far an unmasked loss would dilute that coefficient. Notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} counts both under two target policies on the same input.

```{python}
#| label: lego-15-selected-target-accounting
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTED TARGET ACCOUNTING (LEGO)
# │ Context: @nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation.
# │ Goal: Separate stored positions from eligible imitation targets.
# │ Show: Two masks on one hypothetical input retain identical context.
# │ How: Sum segment counts; exclude unselected responses; count targets.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class SelectedTargetAccounting:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical Token Counts) ────────────────────────────
    prompt = 1_200  # includes the initial context/boundary position
    task = 184
    optional_rationale = 1_400  # available, authorized, reviewed text
    response = 960  # response content and authentic terminators
    observation = 12_640
    unselected_response = 160  # retained as context, not desired targets
    checkpoint_observation = 30_000  # given for the reader's estimate in the checkpoint

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (One Input, Two Target Policies) ────────────────────
    stored = prompt + task + optional_rationale + response + observation
    selected_response = response - unselected_response
    with_rationale = selected_response + optional_rationale
    without_rationale = selected_response
    observation_share = observation / stored
    with_share = with_rationale / stored
    without_share = without_rationale / stored
    context_only_with = stored - with_rationale
    context_only_without = stored - without_rationale
    # Unmasked token averaging divides by every stored position instead.
    dilution_without = stored / without_rationale
    dilution_with = stored / with_rationale
    stored_double_obs = stored + observation
    dilution_double_obs = stored_double_obs / without_rationale
    unselected_vs_selected = unselected_response / selected_response

    # ┌── 3. ASSERT (Partitions and Positive Denominators) ───────────────
    check(0 <= unselected_response < response, "valid response selection")
    check(stored == 16_384, "declared input partition")
    check(0 < without_rationale <= with_rationale < stored, "valid targets")
    check(with_rationale + context_only_with == stored, "first partition")
    check(without_rationale + context_only_without == stored, "second partition")
    check(with_rationale - without_rationale == optional_rationale, "mask difference")
    check(dilution_without > dilution_with > 1, "masking concentrates weight")
    check(dilution_double_obs > dilution_without, "longer observations dilute more")
    check(checkpoint_observation > observation, "checkpoint grows the observations")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Computed Display Exports) ───────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    task_str = fmt_int(task)
    rationale_str = fmt_int(optional_rationale)
    response_str = fmt_int(response)
    observation_str = fmt_int(observation)
    unselected_str = fmt_int(unselected_response)
    stored_str = fmt_int(stored)
    observation_share_str = fmt_percent(observation_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    with_str = fmt_int(with_rationale)
    without_str = fmt_int(without_rationale)
    with_share_str = fmt_percent(with_share, precision=1, style="symbol")
    without_share_str = fmt_percent(without_share, precision=1, style="symbol")
    selected_response_str = fmt_int(selected_response)
    dilution_without_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_without, precision=1)
    dilution_with_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_with, precision=1)
    dilution_double_obs_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_double_obs, precision=1)
    unselected_vs_selected_str = fmt_percent(unselected_vs_selected, precision=0, style="prose")
    checkpoint_observation_str = fmt_int(checkpoint_observation)
```

::: {#nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation .callout-notebook title="Stored tokens and selected targets"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical serialized example has the segment counts in @tbl-vol3-mask-token-inventory. Its curation record excludes some policy-response positions from imitation while retaining them as context. If the optional rationale is either selected or kept as context only, how many positions receive direct loss, what fraction of the stored input do they occupy, and by how much would an unmasked loss dilute each of them?

| Input segment                                             |                                       Stored tokens |
|:----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------:|
| System prompt and schemas, including the initial boundary |      `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.prompt_str` |
| Task statement                                            |        `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.task_str` |
| Optional authorized rationale                             |   `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.rationale_str` |
| Other policy responses, including authentic end tokens    |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.response_str` |
| Delivered observations                                    | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.observation_str` |

: **Hypothetical Input Inventory**: These disjoint counts include every stored position. They are not measurements of the shared repair run. {#tbl-vol3-mask-token-inventory}

**Variables**: Exactly `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.unselected_str` of the other-policy-response positions belong to the refused proposal and stay context; every other response position is selected. The rationale is reviewed for either target policy, both policies see the same input, the initial position belongs to the prompt, and there is no padding.

**Math**: The disjoint segments sum to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.stored_str` stored tokens, of which observations occupy `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.observation_share_str`. Removing the refused positions leaves `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.response_str` $-$ `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.unselected_str` $=$ `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.selected_response_str` selected response targets, and selecting the rationale adds `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.rationale_str` more. An unmasked token average divides by all `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.stored_str` positions instead of $N_{\mathrm{active}}$, so each selected target's coefficient shrinks by `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.stored_str`/`{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.selected_response_str`, a factor of `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_without_mult_str` (`{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_with_mult_str` when the rationale is selected).

| Target policy                                          |       Selected positions, $N_{\mathrm{active}}$ |                        Selected share of stored input |
|:-------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------------:|
| Selected responses plus reviewed rationale             |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.with_str` |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.with_share_str` |
| Selected responses; rationale retained as context only | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.without_str` | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.without_share_str` |

: **Two Target Policies on One Input**: Excluding a segment from the objective does not shorten the conditioning sequence. {#tbl-vol3-mask-target-counts}

**Result**: Both masks in @tbl-vol3-mask-target-counts place the whole loss on a small minority of stored positions and leave the context identical; they differ only in whether the rationale is a target.

**Systems insight**: The dilution factor is the inverse of the selected share, so it grows with observation length. Doubling the observation text while the responses stay fixed raises it from `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_without_mult_str` to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_double_obs_mult_str`. Masking therefore matters most for exactly the long, tool-heavy trajectories agents produce. The compute it saves stays small, because every masked token is still processed as context for the selected predictions after it; the output-head and loss work at masked positions is the only part a loader can skip.

:::

### Optional rationale as target or context {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-optional-rationale}

The repair demonstration needs no private or hidden reasoning trace. Where a dataset includes authorized generated rationale, its treatment is a separate choice. Selecting rationale as in @tbl-vol3-reasoning-mask-regimes trains the policy to predict that text. Masking it retains the same conditioning information but removes its direct prediction loss. Removing it changes the input and therefore the conditional prediction problem.

For a supplied prefix $c$, retained rationale $\rho$, and response tokens $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, response-only supervision trains factors $P_\theta(a_j\mid c,\rho,a_{<j})$. A deployment that supplies no $\rho$ instead uses $P_\theta(a_j\mid c,a_{<j})$. These are different conditional problems, so removing rationale during training is a declared distillation experiment, measured on the second problem.

| Treatment                                        | Input and direct targets                                            | Serving question to evaluate                                                                          |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Select reviewed rationale                        | Retain $[c,\rho,a]$; selected $\rho$ and $a$ positions receive loss | Does generated rationale improve the declared outcomes enough to justify its output and latency cost? |
| Retain rationale as context only                 | Retain $[c,\rho,a]$; only selected $a$ positions receive loss       | How will appropriate rationale become available, and how do errors in it affect the response?         |
| Remove rationale under a reviewed transformation | Use $[c,a]$; selected $a$ positions receive loss                    | Does the policy perform adequately without the removed conditioning information?                      |

: **Rationale Treatment Changes Targets or Inputs**: The choice requires a compatible serving protocol and evaluation, not a universal model-size threshold. {#tbl-vol3-reasoning-mask-regimes}

A policy with existing rationale-generation ability can itself provide the retained text at serving time, as can an upstream planner. Its generated rationale can differ from the demonstrated text, and evaluation measures that mismatch. A rationale earns target status from the declared evidence and use policy, not from having preceded a successful correction.

### Termination and truncated responses {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-termination}

For a selected complete response, the template's authentic policy-generated end token or end sequence can teach where that response should stop. Keep it distinct from a delimiter inserted by the host to introduce the next tool message. Omitting a desired termination target removes that example's direct supervision of stopping, and runtime limits bound generation under either mask.

A cut-off response has no terminator to select. The error is appending a synthetic end marker and labeling the fragment a complete desired response. A conservative policy excludes the unfinished response's targets and keeps earlier eligible responses. A deliberate partial-response policy can instead select justified prefix tokens, provided it preserves the truncation status, supplies no false completion target, and has the earlier context those tokens need.

After truncation, transformation, or splitting, recompute both the target alignment and the positive active count. Inspect boundary cases: the first selected response token, a genuine termination token, the first tool observation token, a masked earlier error, and a cut-off call. These checks test whether the loader implements the declared learning problem; task completion is measured later, in closed loop.

::: {#chk-15-loss-masking .callout-checkpoint title="Defend the target mask"}

- [ ] **Curation to tokens**: Which of `e2`, `e3`, the tool reply to `e3`, `e4`, and `e6` carry $m_t=1$ under `recovery_targets_v1`, and what would training the others teach?
- [ ] **Causal alignment**: Which input position's logits predict the first selected response token, and which token's mask must accompany that prediction?
- [ ] **Masked versus removed**: How can a masked observation affect parameter updates through a later selected response?
- [ ] **Dilution estimate**: If the observations in notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} grew to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.checkpoint_observation_str` tokens with every other segment unchanged, by roughly what factor would an unmasked token average dilute each selected response target, and why would masking save far less compute than that factor?
- [ ] **Termination**: A response was cut off at the output limit. Which of its positions can you still select, and what must the loader refuse to append?

:::

The mask now identifies which positions contribute direct loss and preserves the input needed to predict them, one example at a time. A training step combines many examples of very different lengths, and the way it combines them must preserve that target contract rather than silently redefine it.

## Batching Variable-Length Trajectories {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching}

Suppose the repair demonstration shares a training buffer with an unrelated file lookup. Under an ordinary causal mask, the lookup's predictions can attend to the repair's file contents and test output, context the lookup will never have when served. Under token averaging, the long repair trace also outweighs the short lookup by the ratio of their selected-token counts. A batch therefore makes two decisions, how much each example contributes to the objective and how examples share storage without sharing information. Packing is only a storage layout, and a correct implementation leaves both the intended loss and each prediction's visible context unchanged.

### Loss normalization across variable-length examples {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-normalization}

Let a batch contain $M$ examples. Example $j$ has stored length $T_j$, including context, and $N_{\mathrm{active},j}>0$ selected target tokens under the preceding section's mask. Let $\ell_j$ be its mean masked negative log-likelihood. Two batch objectives are

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{token}}=
\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{N_{\mathrm{active},j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}N_{\mathrm{active},k}}\ell_j,$$ {#eq-vol3-loss-token}

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{example}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\ell_j.$$ {#eq-vol3-loss-example}

**Token averaging**\index{Token averaging!definition} in @eq-vol3-loss-token assigns equal coefficients to selected token losses. **Example averaging**\index{Example averaging!definition} in @eq-vol3-loss-example assigns equal coefficients to example means. Both count selected targets, never context or padding. A record with no selected targets supplies no $\ell_j$ and is excluded from either objective.

The coefficients weight losses; gradient magnitudes also depend on prediction errors and parameter sensitivities. Example averaging weights tasks only through their examples. Splitting one trajectory into $H$ per-invocation examples, as serialization sometimes requires, multiplies its weight by $H$ under example averaging and leaves it unchanged under token averaging when each example selects only its own turn's response. Sampling, segmentation, and normalization therefore set task weighting jointly.

| Property                             | Token averaging                                      | Example averaging             |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| Coefficient on example mean $\ell_j$ | $N_{\mathrm{active},j}/\sum_k N_{\mathrm{active},k}$ | $1/M$                         |
| Coefficient on a selected token loss | $1/\sum_k N_{\mathrm{active},k}$                     | $1/(M N_{\mathrm{active},j})$ |
| Quantity treated equally             | Selected token losses                                | Example mean losses           |

: **Loss normalization for variable-length examples**: Equal coefficients specify the objective, not equal gradient norms or equal representation of underlying tasks. {#tbl-vol3-loss-normalization-comparison}

The coefficients in @tbl-vol3-loss-normalization-comparison must survive implementation. A global token mean sums selected-token losses and counts across microbatches before dividing; averaging microbatch means equally reproduces it only when their counts match. Distributed workers need the same summed counts.

### Example isolation in packed buffers {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-packed-isolation}

::: {#dfn-sequence-packing .callout-definition title="Sequence packing"}

***Sequence packing***\index{Sequence packing!definition} places several variable-length training examples in shared buffers while preserving their intended information boundaries and loss targets.

1. **Significance**: Padding allocates the longest example's length to every row, so a padded batch's occupancy falls to its mean-to-maximum length ratio; packing recovers most of that space (notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-packing-occupancy}).
2. **Distinction**: Independent examples share storage, not predictive context; turns within one example still attend to their earlier history.
3. **Common pitfall**: Applying an ordinary causal mask to concatenated independent examples, allowing later examples to attend to earlier ones.

:::

The lookup from the section's opening must never read the repair's file contents or tool observations, the *cross-contamination*[^fn-packing-cross-contamination] that a packed layout must prevent [@krell2021efficient]. Let $i$ and $j$ denote buffer positions, $Q_i$ and $K_j$ their query and key vectors, and $d$ the attention-head dimension. The pre-softmax attention scores $\mathrm{score}_{i,j}$ enforce both causality and example membership:

$$\mathrm{score}_{i,j}=\begin{cases}
Q_iK_j^{\top}/\sqrt d & \text{if }\operatorname{example}(i)=\operatorname{example}(j)\text{ and }j\le i,\\
-\infty & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$ {#eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention}

@Fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask draws @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention for two packed examples beside the ordinary causal mask it replaces, a pattern called **block-diagonal attention**\index{Block-diagonal attention!definition}. Padding keys are excluded as well. Boundary offsets identify each example's interval, so a kernel can apply the mask from that metadata without allocating a dense matrix, and a variable-length attention kernel can also skip the masked cross-example blocks. That skipped work, rather than the mask itself, is where any compute saving comes from.

[^fn-packing-cross-contamination]: **Cross-Contamination**: Krell and colleagues used the term for attention and label leakage between sequences packed into one buffer, and showed that masks, position resets, and per-sequence loss handling make a packed model mathematically equivalent to the unpacked one. The equivalence is the property to test: a packed loader that trains faster but lets examples read one another has changed the learning problem, and no loss curve will show it.

::: {#fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property." fig-alt="Two eight-by-eight attention grids, queries down the side and keys across the top, each split into example 1 with five positions and example 2 with three. In panel a, the lower triangle within each example is shaded as a score, the upper triangle is marked minus infinity, and the block where example 2 queries meet example 1 keys is shaded red as a cross-example score. In panel b, the same lower triangles are shaded, and the whole cross-example block is marked minus infinity. A legend defines the score, minus infinity before softmax, and cross-example score."}
![](images/svg/ch13-block-diagonal-mask.svg)
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_sft_margin_occupancy.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars. The upper bar, labeled packed 76.6%, is about four times longer than the lower bar, labeled padded 19.1%."}

*One long trajectory holds padded occupancy to 19.1 percent; packing reaches 76.6 percent.*
:::

Loss construction needs the same boundaries. Shifting labels across the entire concatenated buffer can accidentally train the last position of one example to predict the first token of the next. Each example's initial context seed remains unselected, as in the preceding mask definition, and shifted prediction-target pairs must stay inside their example. Attention masks and target masks enforce different constraints; both must be correct.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-packing-occupancy
#| echo: false
# PACKING OCCUPANCY (LEGO)
# Goal: Compare stored-token occupancy, not measured training throughput.
# Scope: Hypothetical independent examples and two fixed-capacity buffers.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class PackingOccupancy:
    # 1. LOAD: stored lengths and a separate two-example weighting illustration.
    lengths = [32768, 8192, 4096, 2048, 1024, 1024, 512, 512]
    capacity = 32768
    active_short = 256
    active_long = 8192

    # 2. EXECUTE: the longest example occupies one buffer; all others fit another.
    stored = sum(lengths)
    padded = len(lengths) * max(lengths)
    second_buffer = sum(lengths[1:])
    packed = 2 * capacity
    padded_occupancy = stored / padded
    packed_occupancy = stored / packed
    position_ratio = padded / packed
    mean_length = stored / len(lengths)
    coefficient_ratio = active_long / active_short
    short_weight = active_short / (active_short + active_long)
    long_weight = active_long / (active_short + active_long)

    # 3. GUARD: feasible layout and distinct normalization coefficients.
    check(max(lengths) == capacity, "Longest example fits exactly")
    check(0 < second_buffer <= capacity, "Remaining examples fit second buffer")
    check(0 < stored <= packed <= padded, "Occupancy bounds")
    check(abs(short_weight + long_weight - 1) < 1e-12, "Token weights sum to one")
    check(active_short > 0 and active_long > 0, "Nonempty target sets")
    check(abs(padded_occupancy - mean_length / max(lengths)) < 1e-12, "Padded occupancy is mean/max")

    # 4. OUTPUT: consumed in the worked calculation.
    stored_str = fmt_int(stored)
    padded_str = fmt_int(padded)
    second_buffer_str = fmt_int(second_buffer)
    packed_str = fmt_int(packed)
    padded_pct_str = fmt_percent(padded_occupancy, precision=1, style="prose")
    packed_pct_str = fmt_percent(packed_occupancy, precision=1, style="prose")
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(position_ratio, precision=0)
    coefficient_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(coefficient_ratio, precision=0)
    mean_str = fmt_int(mean_length)
    max_str = fmt_int(max(lengths))
    short_pct_str = fmt_percent(short_weight, precision=2, style="prose")
    long_pct_str = fmt_percent(long_weight, precision=2, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-packing-occupancy .callout-notebook title="Stored occupancy and target weighting"}

**Problem**: A batch holds one long trajectory among short ones. How much allocated sequence space does packing save over padding, and how differently do the two normalizations weight a long and a short example?

**Variables**: Eight hypothetical examples have stored lengths $[32{,}768,\ 8{,}192,\ 4{,}096,\ 2{,}048,\ 1{,}024,\ 1{,}024,\ 512,\ 512]$. Each packed buffer holds $32{,}768$ positions. Separately, two examples have $256$ and $8{,}192$ selected targets.

**Math**: Padding eight rows to the maximum allocates $8\times32{,}768$ positions, or `{python} PackingOccupancy.padded_str`, for `{python} PackingOccupancy.stored_str` stored tokens. Packing puts the longest example alone and the remaining `{python} PackingOccupancy.second_buffer_str` tokens in a second buffer. The two buffers allocate $2\times32{,}768$ positions, or `{python} PackingOccupancy.packed_str`. Dividing stored tokens by allocated positions gives an occupancy of `{python} PackingOccupancy.padded_pct_str` with padding, which equals the mean length of `{python} PackingOccupancy.mean_str` divided by the maximum of `{python} PackingOccupancy.max_str`, and `{python} PackingOccupancy.packed_pct_str` with packing. Packing allocates `{python} PackingOccupancy.ratio_mult_str` fewer positions.

For the separate target-count illustration, token averaging gives coefficients $256/(256+8{,}192)$ and $8{,}192/(256+8{,}192)$, or `{python} PackingOccupancy.short_pct_str` and `{python} PackingOccupancy.long_pct_str` on the example means. Their ratio, $8{,}192/256$, is `{python} PackingOccupancy.coefficient_ratio_mult_str`. Example averaging instead assigns each mean $1/2$.

**Systems insight**: Padded occupancy is the ratio of mean to maximum length, so the single longest trajectory sets the waste: one `{python} PackingOccupancy.max_str`-token example holds this batch to `{python} PackingOccupancy.padded_pct_str`, and packing raises it to `{python} PackingOccupancy.packed_pct_str`. Occupancy counts context and targets together, so the throughput it buys is measured on the actual attention kernel. Normalization is a separate knob with an equally large effect. Token averaging gives the long example `{python} PackingOccupancy.coefficient_ratio_mult_str` the short one's weight, and example averaging gives them equal weight. Choose token averaging when every selected token should count equally, and example averaging when a few long trajectories should not dominate the update.

:::

### Position conventions and equivalence checks {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-position-conventions}

An implementation must also preserve the model's intended position convention. A common convention resets positions at each example boundary. For zero-based buffer offsets $b_k$ and $b_{k+1}$ bounding example $k$,

$$\operatorname{pos}[t]=t-b_k\quad\text{for }t\in[b_k,b_{k+1}).$$

For rotary position embeddings (RoPE), resetting is a convention rather than a mathematical requirement. In the fixed-frequency formulation, position $i$ applies a rotation $R_i$ to a query or key. Shifting both positions by a common offset $b$ leaves their relative rotation unchanged:

$$R_{i+b}^{\top}R_{j+b}=R_{j-i}=R_i^{\top}R_j.$$

A common offset therefore leaves within-example attention scores unchanged, a consequence of the relative-position construction of RoPE [@su2024]. Absolute-position features, position-dependent scaling, and numerical precision can still break equivalence for a particular model, and the following test detects them.

The correctness test compares selected-token logits and the declared loss for the same examples processed separately and packed, with stochastic layers disabled and numerical tolerances stated. Perturbing one example must leave every other example's logits unchanged. The test exercises attention boundaries, label shifting, position IDs, and the chosen denominator together. When it passes, the loader trains exactly the demonstrated problem. The trained policy, however, acts in contexts its own choices produce.

## Exposure Bias {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-exposure-bias}

Suppose a fresh bounded trial of the trained repair policy meets a version conflict instead of the malformed-argument rejection recorded in `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`. The policy repeats the previously accepted edit without obtaining compatible evidence, the conditional-update guard blocks the stale write, and the trial spends its allowance without completing the repair. The corpus never showed that state. Serialization and masking preserve the demonstrated decision problem, but deployment decides which problems the policy meets, and a policy trained by teacher forcing never sees its own mistakes among its inputs. In text generation a mistake only drifts the phrasing. In an agent it changes the environment, so after one call departs from the demonstration every later observation can come from a state the corpus never covered.

::: {#dfn-15-exposure-bias .callout-definition title="Exposure bias"}

***Exposure bias***\index{Exposure bias!definition} is the mismatch between training a sequential policy on reference prefixes and running it on prefixes produced by its own earlier outputs [@bengio2015scheduledsampling; @ranzato2016sequence].

1. **Significance**: It turns a per-step error rate into a horizon-dependent cost. Measured on reference states, an error rate $\epsilon$ bounds excess task cost only by $H^2\epsilon$ (theorem \ref{thrm-15-imitation-regret}), a second factor of $H$ on top of the compounding of @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic.
2. **Distinction**: It is a property of the training distribution rather than of any single mistake. A policy can err on states the corpus covers and recover on states it never showed.
3. **Common pitfall**: Reading low validation loss on recorded prefixes as evidence about the states the trained policy reaches, which that loss never samples.

:::

Offline data can include recoveries, and a policy that departs from the demonstration can return to a familiar state or find another valid solution. Exposure bias[^fn-exposure-bias-lineage] is therefore a question of how well the corpus covers the states the trained policy itself visits, the version conflict among them.

[^fn-exposure-bias-lineage]: **Exposure Bias**: Ranzato and colleagues introduced the name in 2016 for text generators trained on reference words and run on their own [@ranzato2016sequence]. Control researchers had met the same effect earlier as the compounding error of behavioral cloning, which Ross and Bagnell bounded in 2010 [@ross2010efficient]. The two literatures describe one mechanism, and agents inherit the control version: a wrong action changes the environment, not just the phrasing.

### State distributions and imitation regret {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-imitation-regret}

An idealized finite-horizon model makes the coverage question precise. Its symbols follow the imitation-learning literature and are local to this derivation. The index $t$ now counts decision steps rather than token positions. The state $s$ is the full environment state of the decision process, which includes whatever history defines it and can hold environment variables the model never saw, unlike the context state $s_t$ in the masking definition (\ref{dfn-action-loss-masking}). Let $H$ be the number of decision steps, $\pi$ the learned policy (written bare because it is held fixed in the argument), and $\pi^*$ a deterministic reference policy, with the same initial-state distribution and environment dynamics. The *state distribution* $d_\pi^t$ is the distribution of states before step $t$ under $\pi$, and $d_\pi=H^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^H d_\pi^t$ averages it over the horizon.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_sft_margin_regret.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two curves over horizon from 0 to H equals 30. A red curve rises quadratically to a dot labeled H squared epsilon equals 18. A blue line stays near the axis and ends at a dot labeled u H epsilon equals 0.6. The gap between them is shaded."}

*Same 2 percent error: 18 cost units on reference states, 0.6 on learner states.*
:::

Let $C(s,a)\in[0,1]$ be a normalized immediate task cost and $J(\pi)$ its expected sum over the horizon. Let $\ell(s,\pi)=\Pr_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}[a\ne\pi^*(s)]$ measure disagreement with the reference. Disagreement is a conservative stand-in for failure, since several actions can be acceptable, and it is a probability of choosing a different action, a different quantity from the token cross-entropy the training job reports. Finally, the *cost-to-go* $Q_t^{\pi^*}(s,a)$ is the expected cost from step $t$ through $H$ after taking $a$ in $s$ and following the reference thereafter.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-sft-distribution-bounds
#| echo: false
# CONDITIONAL COST BOUNDS (LEGO)
# Goal: Show which assumptions distinguish expert-state and learner-state bounds.
# Scope: Hypothetical normalized costs; not observed repair performance.
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class DistributionBounds:
    # 1. LOAD: stipulated horizon, equal numerical errors on different distributions.
    horizon = 30
    epsilon_expert = 0.02
    epsilon_learner = 0.02
    local_disadvantage = 1.0

    # 2. EXECUTE: excess cost cannot exceed the bounded total horizon cost.
    horizon_sq = horizon * horizon
    expert_bound = min(horizon, horizon_sq * epsilon_expert)
    local_bound = min(horizon, local_disadvantage * horizon * epsilon_learner)
    horizon_disadvantage_bound = min(horizon, horizon_sq * epsilon_learner)
    bound_gap = expert_bound / local_bound
    # Reference-state error needed to match the learner-state bound.
    epsilon_matching = local_bound / horizon_sq
    # Horizon at which H^2 eps reaches the cap H and the bound stops constraining cost.
    saturation_horizon = 1 / epsilon_expert

    # 3. GUARD: these are bounds under distinct assumptions, not measured costs.
    check(expert_bound == 18, "Expert-distribution cost bound")
    check(abs(local_bound - 0.6) < 1e-12, "Learner-distribution bound with u=1")
    check(horizon_disadvantage_bound == expert_bound, "No linear gain when u=H")
    check(0 <= local_bound <= expert_bound <= horizon, "Bounded cost range")
    check(abs(bound_gap - horizon / local_disadvantage) < 1e-9, "Gap is H/u")
    check(saturation_horizon > horizon, "Stipulated horizon is below saturation")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every formatted export is used in the theorem or notebook.
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    horizon_sq_str = fmt_int(horizon_sq)
    error_str = fmt_percent(epsilon_expert, precision=0, style="prose")
    error_dec_str = fmt(epsilon_expert, precision=2)
    u_str = fmt_int(local_disadvantage)
    expert_str = fmt_int(expert_bound)
    local_str = fmt(local_bound, precision=1)
    horizon_bound_str = fmt_int(horizon_disadvantage_bound)
    gap_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bound_gap, precision=0)
    matching_str = fmt_percent(epsilon_matching, precision=2, style="prose")
    saturation_str = fmt_int(saturation_horizon)
```

::: {#thrm-15-imitation-regret .callout-theorem title="Imitation regret bounds"}

*The horizon penalty of imitation depends on which states the error is measured on.* For a policy $\pi$ imitating a deterministic reference $\pi^*$ over $H$ steps with per-step cost in $[0,1]$, @ross2011reduction bound the excess task cost in two ways.

**Reference-state error** (their Theorem 2.1, first proved by @ross2010efficient). With disagreement measured on the reference policy's states, $\epsilon_E=\mathbb E_{s\sim d_{\pi^*}}[\ell(s,\pi)]$,

$$J(\pi)-J(\pi^*)\le \min\{H,\;H^2\epsilon_E\}.$$ {#eq-vol3-quadratic-derivation}

**Learner-state error** (their Theorem 2.2). With disagreement measured on the learner's states, $\epsilon_\pi=\mathbb E_{s\sim d_\pi}[\ell(s,\pi)]$, and every deviation followed by reference recovery costing at most $u$ extra, $Q_t^{\pi^*}(s,a)-Q_t^{\pi^*}(s,\pi^*(s))\le u$ at every learner-reachable state,

$$J(\pi)-J(\pi^*)\le \min\{H,\;uH\epsilon_\pi\}.$$ {#eq-vol3-linear-regret-bound}

* **Horizon** ($H$): decision steps in the task; because each step costs at most one, $H$ also caps both bounds.
* **State distributions** ($d_{\pi^*}$, $d_\pi$): the environment states the reference or the learner visits, averaged over the horizon.
* **Disagreement rates** ($\epsilon_E$, $\epsilon_\pi$): probability of an action other than the reference's, averaged over reference-visited or learner-visited states.
* **Deviation disadvantage**\index{Deviation disadvantage!definition} ($u\ge0$): the largest extra expected cost of one deviation followed by reference recovery, an assumption about the task rather than a measured retry count.

The same error rate therefore carries different horizon penalties. At $H=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_str` and a `{python} DistributionBounds.error_str` disagreement rate, the reference-state bound is `{python} DistributionBounds.expert_str` cost units and the learner-state bound with $u=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.u_str` is `{python} DistributionBounds.local_str`, a gap of `{python} DistributionBounds.gap_mult_str`, which is $H/u$. The linear bound holds only while $u$ stays independent of $H$; one action that can spoil the rest of the task makes $u$ grow with $H$ and restores the quadratic dependence.

:::

The quadratic term has a direct reading. Couple the environment randomness of the two policies until they first choose different actions. The probability of any such divergence is at most the sum of disagreement probabilities along the reference process, $H\epsilon_E$, and a divergence can affect as much as the whole remaining horizon. The coupling argument makes no assumption about the learner's error rate after it first diverges. @Sec-vol3-appendix-math-compounding-error derives the reference-state bound by coupling and the learner-state bound through telescoping policy comparisons.

@Sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic showed unchecked step errors compounding as $(1-\epsilon)^H$ at run time. Theorem \ref{thrm-15-imitation-regret} is the training-side counterpart, in which imitation measured on the wrong distribution pays a second factor of $H$. Recovery records help exactly insofar as they move the measured error onto learner-visited states and keep $u$ small, and a corpus alone cannot show that either assumption holds.

::: {#nbk-15-quantifying-trajectory-collapse-and-dagger .callout-notebook title="The same error rate under different assumptions"}

**Problem**: An illustrative task has horizon `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_str` and immediate cost bounded between zero and one. Compare a `{python} DistributionBounds.error_str` disagreement rate on reference-policy states with the same numerical rate on learner-policy states. What changes if the latter also satisfies a deviation-disadvantage bound of $u=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.u_str`, and how accurate would offline imitation have to be to match it?

**Math**: The reference-state bound multiplies $H^2=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_sq_str` by $\epsilon_E=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.error_dec_str`, giving `{python} DistributionBounds.expert_str` normalized cost units, below the cap of `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_str`. The learner-state bound multiplies $u H=$ `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_str` by the same rate, giving `{python} DistributionBounds.local_str`. If the disadvantage instead reaches $u=H$, the learner bound returns to `{python} DistributionBounds.horizon_bound_str`. Matching the learner-state bound on reference states requires $\epsilon_E$ equal to that bound divided by $H^2$, about `{python} DistributionBounds.matching_str`.

**Result**: At this horizon the two bounds differ by `{python} DistributionBounds.gap_mult_str` for the same measured error rate.

**Systems insight**: The gap is $H/u$, so it grows linearly with the horizon. Offline imitation must be $H/u$ times more accurate on reference states to carry the guarantee that labeling learner-visited states provides. The reference-state bound also saturates at its cap once $H\ge 1/\epsilon_E$, here `{python} DistributionBounds.saturation_str` steps, beyond which it constrains nothing. Long-horizon agents with cheap, recoverable deviations are therefore where on-policy labeling pays most. When one deviation can spoil the task ($u$ near $H$), the learner-state bound is no better than the quadratic one, and the runtime checks of principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure} carry the reliability.

:::

### Dataset aggregation {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dagger}

**Dataset Aggregation (DAgger)**\index{DAgger!definition} collects trajectories under successive learned policies, obtains reference actions at the states they visit, aggregates those labeled examples, and retrains[^fn-dagger-mixing-schedule] [@ross2011reduction]. The result is **on-policy data**\index{On-policy data!definition}, examples drawn from the state distribution of the policy being trained. Executing a learner action and requesting its reference label are different operations, and early rounds mix them. In round $k$ the collector executes the reference action with probability $\lambda_k$ and the learner's action otherwise, decaying $\lambda_k$ toward zero so the collected states shift gradually toward the learner's own distribution. That shift is what moves the measured error onto learner states and makes the learner-state bound of theorem \ref{thrm-15-imitation-regret} the applicable one.

[^fn-dagger-mixing-schedule]: **DAgger's Mixing Schedule**: Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell require only that the average reference-execution probability tend to zero over rounds, and report that the simplest schedule, executing the reference only in the first round, often performs best. The systems cost sits elsewhere: every visited state needs a reference label on demand, so the labeler is an online service in the collection loop rather than a one-time annotation pass.

The version conflict is exactly such a state, and for the repair agent the practical question is whether an authorized labeler can supply a justified response there. The labeler, usually a stronger model or a larger test-time budget, produces a proposal like any other, and a wrong label trains recovery in the wrong direction. The pipeline therefore continues the trajectory from the corrected action in a sandbox and keeps the label only if the task's verifier accepts the outcome under the consumer-specific predicates of @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation. An accepted continuation shows that the label works, not that it is the only action that would. Labeling extends beyond detected errors, since a superficially successful step can also be poorly grounded, and it preserves the actual observations, the current tool contract, and any unavailable or disputed labels.

Retraining changes the policy and with it the states it visits, so the resulting policy is evaluated on new bounded trials and the protected task set, not on the aggregate training sample, which describes earlier rounds' distributions. The broader collection and selection feedback belongs to @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-self-improvement.

**Fault injection**\index{Fault injection!training data} supplies a complementary source of declared conditions. The injected error is an observation with $m_t=0$; the diagnosis and the corrective call are selected targets with $m_t=1$. That places direct loss on exactly the off-path decision a demonstrated path never exercises. The correction targets must retain matching observations and effect semantics, including the distinction between a refusal before dispatch and a lost acknowledgment after a possible effect. Fault injection covers the failures the fixture anticipates, and on-policy collection covers the ones only the policy's own behavior reveals. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) differs from both, because it learns from fresh reward-scored outcomes and needs no corrective reference action at each state (@sec-vol3-rlvr). @Fig-vol3-exposure-bias-dagger contrasts training on recorded reference states with this collection loop.

::: {#fig-vol3-exposure-bias-dagger fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling**: Training only on recorded reference states (a) leaves any state the learner reaches after a deviation without a recorded correction, and the applicable bound, @eq-vol3-quadratic-derivation, grows with $H^2\epsilon_E$. Each labeling round (b) runs the current policy, mixed with the reference at probability $\lambda_k$, labels the states it visits, keeps a label only if the sandbox continuation passes the verifier, aggregates, and retrains. A fault-injected record masks the injected error and selects the diagnosis and corrective call. The bound in @eq-vol3-linear-regret-bound applies only when error is measured on learner states and each deviation's disadvantage is bounded by $u$; aggregation broadens coverage but does not by itself make the training and learner distributions equal." fig-alt="Two stacked panels.
